# Full review of the thesis: findings

> **Status: incomplete run (2026-10-23).** The review stopped at the weekly usage limit before it finished. All six reviewers ran on all 15 units and all 15 whole-thesis passes ran. Only the findings of the whole-thesis passes went through the three-lens verification (text, rule, sceptic); every finding marked "verification incomplete" (2,085 of 2,346) is a raw reviewer finding: not checked by the verifiers, not merged across reviewers within its unit (except Front matter), and its severity is the reviewer's own. The completeness rounds (except Front matter), the prerequisite ledger, the terminology table, severity calibration, the fix-first list, the cross-cutting themes and the reviewer paragraphs did not run. Expect duplicates (the same problem reported by several reviewers) and some false positives among the unverified findings. **Update:** the S1 and S2 findings were verified afterwards in the main session: see [03-verification-S1-S2.md](03-verification-S1-S2.md) (246 confirmed problems: 13 S1, 122 S2, 111 downgraded to S3; 1 dropped).

## Findings

### R-0001 · S2 · Title page — main-thesis.tex:190

~~~text
\title{Neural PDE Solvers for Geographic Atrophy Progression Prediction from Longitudinal OCT Imaging}
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Copy editor, Supervisor, External reviewer, Examiner, Colleague
- **Rule:** Guide §5.7 (title plain, no abbreviations; title and abstract agree)
- **Problem:** The title contains two abbreviations (PDE, OCT) and a four-noun stack ('Geographic Atrophy Progression Prediction'). It also names neural PDE solvers, which the abstract never mentions: the abstract speaks of a framework and operators. Title and abstract therefore do not describe the work the same way. (The title is still a working title to be agreed with the supervisor.)
- **Fix:** Spell out the abbreviations, break the noun stack and align the title with the abstract, e.g. "Forecasting the Progression of Geographic Atrophy from Longitudinal Optical Coherence Tomography: Framework and Operators". Needs: the final title agreed with the supervisor.
- **Also at:** main-thesis.tex:193; main-thesis.tex:193; 00-abstract.tex:150; main-thesis.tex:193; 00-abstract.tex:150
- **Recurs:** AI-S21
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0002 · S3 · Title page — main-thesis.tex:190 (p. i)

~~~text
\title{Neural PDE Solvers for Geographic Atrophy Progression Prediction from Longitudinal OCT Imaging}
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Examiner
- **Rule:** Guide §5.7 (title: plain, no abbreviations, states the content without overstating it)
- **Problem:** The title contains two abbreviations (PDE, OCT). It also puts one family of architectures in front, although the thesis's contribution is the framework and the controlled comparison, and its headline is that operators of different classes (including a U-Net) reach similar scores. A reader who sees only the title expects a thesis about neural PDE solvers.
- **Fix:** needs: final title agreed with the supervisor. Possible wording: 'Forecasting Geographic Atrophy Progression from Longitudinal Optical Coherence Tomography: A Controlled Comparison of Learned Operators'.
- **Recurs:** AI-S21
- **Status:** open

### R-0003 · S4 · Title page, keywords (p. i) — main-thesis.tex:238

- **Rule:** Guide §5.7 (keywords should extend the title, not repeat it)
- **Problem:** Three of the seven keywords (Geographic Atrophy, OCT, neural PDE solvers) repeat the title, and "OCT" is an abbreviation. The keywords therefore add few new search terms and give a lopsided picture of the survey.

### R-0009 · S2 · Abstract — 00-abstract.tex:58

~~~text
Geographic Atrophy (GA) is the advanced form of age-related macular
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Clinical reader, External reviewer, Copy editor
- **Rule:** judgement (factual precision of a medical statement); Guide §5.7 (abstract must agree with the text)
- **Problem:** AMD has two late (advanced) forms, neovascular AMD and GA. Section 1.1 says so ("two late forms: neovascular AMD ... and macular atrophy"), and the Kurzfassung correctly says "eine Spätform". "The advanced form" implies that GA is the only advanced form of AMD, so English and German differ in content in their first sentence, and an ophthalmologist notices this at once. The wording follows the supervisor's suggestion SV-A2; only the article is wrong.
- **Fix:** Geographic Atrophy (GA) is the atrophic late form of age-related macular degeneration, manifested as a gradual and irreversible loss of retinal tissue. (Alternatively "an advanced form"; either matches §1.1 and "eine Spätform".)
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0011 · S3 · Abstract — 00-abstract.tex:61

~~~text
will grow would support patient management, but it is difficult to model:
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Supervisor, Copy editor
- **Rule:** Guide §2.4 (simple sentences, clear subject, one idea per sentence)
- **Problem:** Grammatically, 'it is difficult to model' refers to 'a forecast', but what is difficult to model is GA progression (the Kurzfassung says so: 'Die Modellierung dieser Progression'). The sentence also joins the benefit of a forecast and the difficulty of modelling, which the structure I asked for keeps as separate points (problem, then difficulty).

### R-0012 · S3 · Abstract (p. ii) vs Kurzfassung (p. iii-iv) — 00-abstract.tex:64

~~~text
progression from the perspective of computational modelling and determines
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Examiner
- **Rule:** judgement: the English abstract and the Kurzfassung must agree in content (formal requirement)
- **Problem:** The Kurzfassung differs from the English abstract in four statements. (i) "determines what a forecast ... requires" against "untersucht, was ... erfordert" (investigates). (ii) "Neither a fourth-order Runge--Kutta step nor larger models help" (l. 93) against "verbessern die Vorhersage messbar" (measurably); the German matches the null results of §5.6. (iii) "annotated by graders" (l. 76) against "von Befundenden manuell eingezeichnete" (drawn manually, as in §3.1). (iv) "the advanced form of age-related macular degeneration" (l. 58) against "eine Spätform" (a late form); §1.1 names two late forms of AMD. In each case the English is the stronger or less precise version, so a bilingual examiner reads two different claims.
- **Fix:** Align the English with the German: "... and investigates what a forecast from longitudinal optical coherence tomography (OCT) requires"; "Neither a fourth-order Runge--Kutta step nor larger models improve the forecast measurably."; "a binary GA mask, annotated manually by graders". For (iv), either "an advanced form" in English or "die fortgeschrittene Form" in German, whichever the supervisor accepts, so that both say the same and agree with §1.1.
- **Also at:** 00-abstract.tex:93; 00-abstract.tex:76; 00-abstract.tex:58; 00-abstract.tex:129; 00-abstract.tex:168
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0013 · S2 · Abstract — 00-abstract.tex:65

~~~text
what a forecast from longitudinal optical coherence tomography (OCT)
requires: a framework around the model, and an operator inside it that maps
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Supervisor, Colleague
- **Rule:** Guide §11.1 (abstract polished, agrees with the text); judgement (the aim must match the research question of §1.2)
- **Problem:** Read literally, the sentence says the thesis 'determines' that a forecast requires a framework and an operator, which is a trivial answer. It is not the question: §1.2 asks what *kind* of framework and what *kind* of operator are needed. A reader of the abstract alone cannot tell that the two items are the two parts of a question rather than its result.
- **Fix:** "This thesis studies GA progression from the perspective of computational modelling and asks two questions about a forecast from longitudinal optical coherence tomography (OCT): what kind of framework it requires around the model, and what kind of operator, the learned map from one visit to the next, that framework requires." (German l. 129-132 likewise: "... und untersucht, welche Art von Framework ... und welche Art von Operator ... erforderlich ist.")
- **Also at:** 00-abstract.tex:130; 00-abstract.tex:130
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0017 · S2 · Abstract — 00-abstract.tex:70

~~~text
models for GA. The comparison identifies the property that separates them:
whether one update can see as far as the lesion front moves between two
~~~

- **Problem:** The aim paragraph ends on the reveal construction I objected to in Chapter 7 ('What separates ...'): a colon introduces a single clause, and the verb 'see' is figurative. ### R-0018 · S2 · Abstract (English) — 00-abstract.tex:70

~~~text
models for GA. The comparison identifies the property that separates them:
whether one update can see as far as the lesion front moves between two
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** Guide §5.4 (tone down what the data do not carry); Guide §11.5 ("What separates ... is")
- **Problem:** The abstract states reach as an established mechanism and as the difference between operators in general. The body does not. §5.4.5 calls the agreement of the stencil network and the T-FEN "consistent with the reach explanation but does not prove the mechanism". §5.4.2 limits reach to the graph network ("Reach along the rows therefore decides how well the graph network does"). §5.2 places the three highest arms, from three classes, within about 0.04. The FNO sees the whole grid in every layer and still scores below the U-Net (§5.4.3), so reach does not separate the classes. Two later sentences repeat the stronger reading: "Among operators with spatial context, the main difference is reach" (line 93) and "closes the same gap by another mechanism" (line 101). The Kurzfassung repeats it as well. The opening sentence also takes the "X is what separates" form that the supervisor objected to.

### R-0037 · S2 · Abstract (English) — 00-abstract.tex:93

~~~text
fourth-order Runge--Kutta step nor larger models help.
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** Guide §5.8 (methods and results consistent); Guide §5.4 (tone down what the data do not carry)
- **Problem:** The Runge-Kutta null was measured on the dilated-stencil network and the FNO (§5.6.1). The operator called the strongest two sentences earlier, the T-FEN, is always integrated with RK4 in fixed 45-day sub-steps (§4.3.6). One reason is that an explicit Euler step would amplify its transport modes. The other is that its spatial reach comes from the sub-steps. It therefore evaluates its operator many times per visit interval and trains about four times slower than the graph network (367 against 91 s per epoch, Table 5.1). The abstract describes the framework as "the current state plus an update scaled by the time Δt" and the operators as having "similar parameter counts". A reader therefore assumes that all compared operators make the same single update, and the transport result is not read against its different integration. "Larger models" also gives no range: the capacity study spans about a sixth to about four times the original size, at one seed (§5.6.3).
- **Fix:** Replace the sentence by: "For the graph network and the FNO, a fourth-order Runge–Kutta step in place of the single update does not raise the score, and larger models, up to about four times the parameter count, do not score higher. The Finite Element Networks are integrated with Runge–Kutta sub-steps of 45 days by construction." Make the same change in the Kurzfassung (lines 167-168).
- **Also at:** 00-abstract.tex:167
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)

- **Problem:** The explanation reads as "more reach is enough" and leaves out three findings of the body. (i) 11 µm is one hop. The network makes two rounds, so one update reaches about 23 µm (§4.3.3), and that is the quantity the property in lines 70-72 refers to. (ii) The index-space graph reaches about 242 µm across B-scans (§4.3.3), so the stencil also halves the cross-row reach. ### R-0048 · S2 · Abstract (English) — 00-abstract.tex:100

~~~text
0.064 at an identical parameter count, on all five folds. The transport term
closes the same gap by another mechanism (+0.062 over the network without
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement: a second, independent mechanism is claimed that the design in §4.3.6 does not separate; §4.3.6 and §5.4.5 contradict each other
- **Problem:** §4.3.6 says the transport term runs on its own coarser mesh of seven interleaved triangulations, each connecting every seventh column, and calls it "the finite-element counterpart of the dilated stencil". The free-form term and the free-form control use the full-resolution mesh. The comparison behind +0.062 therefore adds the transport term and a mesh with the stencil's seven-column spacing at the same time. It cannot show that transport is "another mechanism" than reach. §1.3 ("two independent routes"), §5.4.5 ("two unrelated constructions"), §6.1.2 and Chapter 7 rest on the same comparison. §4.3.6 also says that the FEN's reach comes from its RK4 sub-steps. Over a 180-day interval these are four steps of four evaluations each, so the printed text does not show that the free-form control has the reach gap the transport term is said to close.
- **Fix:** Reword to what the comparison shows: "A learned transport term, which the Finite Element Network evaluates on a mesh that links every seventh column like the stencil, raises its score by a similar amount (+0.062 over the same network without it)." Before the term is called an independent route (here, and in §1.3, §5.4.5, §6.1.2 and Chapter 7), the thesis needs either a T-FEN run with the transport term on the full-resolution mesh or a statement that the mesh spacing was not varied.

### R-0096 · S4 · §1.1 Clinical Motivation — 01-introduction.tex:17

~~~text
AMD progresses from early and intermediate stages to two late forms: neovascular AMD, with abnormal blood vessel growth, and
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Clinical reader
- **Rule:** Guide §0.2 (say things in the right order)
- **Problem:** The staging runs late forms, then early-stage drusen, then back to the atrophic late form. A clinical reader expects early stages before late ones. 'Macular atrophy' is used as the name of the late form and GA defined right after, so the drusen sentence sits between a term and the definition that builds on it.
- **Fix:** Reorder lines 17-22: "The early stages of AMD are marked by drusen, extracellular deposits of cellular debris \citep{Boyer2017}. From early and intermediate stages, the disease progresses to two late forms: neovascular AMD, with abnormal blood vessel growth, and macular atrophy \citep{Vogl2021}. The atrophic late form without neovascularisation is termed \emph{Geographic Atrophy} (GA)."
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0097 · S2 · §1.1 Clinical Motivation — 01-introduction.tex:21

~~~text
late form without neovascularisation is termed \emph{Geographic Atrophy}
(GA). It is an advanced, irreversible and progressive atrophy of the
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Colleague
- **Rule:** Guide §11.2
- **Problem:** 'Atrophy' is never explained, yet GA, the subject of the thesis, is defined through it ('Geographic Atrophy ... is an ... atrophy of the macula'). For a reader who does not know the word means tissue loss, this definition is circular. 'Macular atrophy' (l. 19) and 'Geographic Atrophy' (l. 21) name the late atrophic form in consecutive sentences without saying how they relate. 'Macular' is used (l. 11, 19) before the macula is defined (l. 23). 'Lesion' (l. 46) then appears without being tied to the atrophic area.
- **Fix:** l. 18-19: "...neovascular AMD, with abnormal blood vessel growth, and macular atrophy, a loss of retinal tissue in the macula, the central region of the retina that provides sharp vision \citep{Vogl2021}." l. 22-23: "It is advanced, irreversible and progressive; the area of lost tissue, called the lesion, enlarges over time."
- **Also at:** 01-introduction.tex:19; 01-introduction.tex:46
- **Recurs:** M2 (supervisor repeat: raised one level)
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

~~~

- **Problem:** Numbers of five or more digits take a thin space as thousands separator in 75 places (67\,147, 50\,176, 1\,394\,273), and four-digit numbers take none (1080 days, 1719 columns, 1536 axial pixels, 1219 eyes, 1000 points). - **Problem:** At least 96 sentences (a heuristic lower bound) use a colon as a hinge between two complete clauses: a full clause before the colon, then an independent clause with its own finite verb that explains or restates it. ### R-0115 · S3 · §1.1 Clinical Motivation — 01-introduction.tex:45

- **Reviewers:** Clinical reader
- **Rule:** judgement (clinical accuracy)
- **Problem:** Mai et al. take this range from a review (their ref. 13). Clinical readers usually know 0.53-2.6 mm²/yr as the spread of mean enlargement rates across studies, not across individual eyes, which vary more widely. ### R-0155 · S2 · §1.2 Aim of the Thesis — 01-introduction.tex:107

~~~text
Such a forecast requires a learned map from the state at one visit to the state at a later one. In this thesis, this map is called the operator.
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** CLAUDE.md: Terminology (one term, one meaning); Guide §4; judgement: definition differs from §2.5.2
- **Problem:** Chapter 1 defines the operator as the map from one state to the next. Equation 2.x of §2.5.2 calls $f_\theta$ the operator. There the state-to-state map is $\mathcal{A}_\theta(\Delta t, u) = u + \Delta t\, f_\theta$, and $f_\theta$ is the term that is multiplied by Δt. For a reader from operator learning these are different objects. The difference matters for the thesis's own claims: $f_\theta$ "cannot be read as a growth rate" (§5.5.1), while the state-to-state map is what is rolled out. In addition, "requires a learned map" is an absolute claim the chapter does not justify.
- **Fix:** Rewrite: "Such a forecast is made here by a learned update that maps the state at one visit to the state at a later one. In this thesis, the learned part of this update, which is added to the current state after scaling by the interval, is called the operator (\S\ref{sec:background:problem})." Also align the §2.5.2 sentence "a map from the state at one time to the state at a later time" with its own equation.
- **Recurs:** SV-X2
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

~~~

### R-0193 · S2 · §1.3 Contributions — 01-introduction.tex:165

~~~text
front and an explicit transport term as two independent routes to the same deficit: a single update that cannot see as far as the lesion front
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement: the stated independence is undercut by the design described in §4.3.6
- **Problem:** The design described in §4.3.6 does not support calling the two routes "independent". The T-FEN's transport term "runs on its own coarser mesh ... each of which connects every seventh column", and the thesis itself calls this mesh "the finite-element counterpart of the dilated stencil". The T-FEN vs free-form comparison therefore adds the transport mechanism and the long reach together. Its +0.062 cannot be credited to transport alone. In addition, "a single update" does not describe the FEN arms. They are always integrated in 45-day RK4 sub-steps (four RK4 steps for a 180-day interval), and §4.3.6 says "spatial reach has to come from sub-steps". So the deficit as stated does not apply to the free-form control in the same way as to the k-NN graph network.
- **Fix:** Drop "independent" and state the confound: "... and an explicit transport term, which in the T-FEN runs on a mesh with the seven-column spacing of the dilated stencil (\S\ref{sec:method:family:fen}), as two constructions that address the same limit: ...". Either qualify "a single update" for the FEN arms ("one evaluation of the operator"), or needs: a T-FEN whose transport term runs on the full-resolution mesh, to separate mechanism from reach.
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0237 · S3 · §2.1.1 Eye Anatomy — 02-background.tex:97

~~~text
\emph{subfoveal} if it overlaps the fovea (i.e.\ it directly threatens
high-acuity vision) and \emph{extrafoveal} otherwise.
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Clinical reader
- **Rule:** judgement (medical term defined imprecisely)
- **Problem:** In GA studies and trials, "subfoveal" means that the lesion involves the foveal centre. A lesion that only overlaps the edge of the 1.5 mm fovea is classed as non-subfoveal (juxtafoveal). A subfoveal lesion has also already reduced central vision; it is the extrafoveal lesion approaching the fovea that "threatens" it. The definition matters because the caption of Figure 3.1(d) uses the term (03-data.tex:148).
- **Fix:** "a lesion is called \emph{subfoveal} if it involves the centre of the fovea, where it directly reduces high-acuity vision, and \emph{extrafoveal} (non-subfoveal) otherwise."
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0295 · S2 · §2.1.3 Geographic Atrophy — 02-background.tex:314

disease in which three tightly coupled \emph{outer}-retinal layers die
together in a localised patch of the macula: the retinal pigment

The RPE and the photoreceptors belong to the outer retina; the choriocapillaris is the innermost layer of the choroid (\S\ref{sec:background:ga-oct:anatomy})." Line 113-114: "that GA destroys the outer retina and the choriocapillaris beneath it in a localised patch (\S\ref{sec:background:ga-oct:disease})".

### R-0299 · S3 · §2.1.3 Geographic Atrophy — 02-background.tex:316

~~~text
epithelium (RPE), the photoreceptor outer segments just above it, and the
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement: inconsistent description of the lost tissue between text and caption
- **Problem:** The thesis describes what GA destroys in three different ways. §2.1.1 (l. 113) and here: "a specific outer-retinal stack of three layers" that "die together": the RPE, the photoreceptor outer segments and the choriocapillaris. Signature (i) (l. 354): the ellipsoid zone and RPE band drop out. Fig. 2.4(b) caption: "the photoreceptors and the RPE are lost and the ONL is reduced to a remnant". Outer segments are parts of the photoreceptor cells, not a layer that dies on its own, and the caption says the cells and their nuclei (ONL) are lost. A reader cannot tell which of the three statements the sources support.

### R-0355 · S3 · §2.2.1 Discretising space: stencils — 02-background.tex:463

~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement (technical error: missing condition)
- **Problem:** With the Galerkin weak form, the semi-discrete system reads M du/dt = r(u). The assembled terms r are local, but the rate at a node is M^{-1} r, and the inverse of the consistent mass matrix is dense, so the rate depends on all nodes. 'The result is again a local stencil' therefore holds only with a lumped (diagonal) mass matrix. That is what the FENs of Lienen and Günnemann and of this thesis use (04-method.tex:983-985, 1002), but §2.2.1 states it as a property of FEM in general. The FEN's reach argument in §4.3.6 ('one evaluation ... only couples nodes that share a triangle') rests on this condition.
- **Fix:** "Because each basis function overlaps only those of its immediate neighbours, the assembled terms couple every node only to the nodes it shares an element with. With a lumped (diagonal) mass matrix, the rate of change at a node is therefore again a local stencil, but one defined by the mesh rather than by a regular grid, which makes the method well suited to irregular domains."

### R-0369 · S2 · §2.2.2 Stepping in time — 02-background.tex:533

~~~text
\emph{consistency}: as the step shrinks to zero, the update must
reproduce the exact solution,
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Examiner
- **Rule:** judgement (mathematical error in a definition the argument builds on); Guide §1 (no absolute claims)
- **Problem:** The definition taken from MP-PDE only asks that A(Δt,u0) → u(Δt) as Δt → 0. Any update with A(0,u) = u satisfies it, including plain persistence. Three statements build on it. (a) The residual form "returns the current state at Δt = 0 whatever the rate" (l. 539). (b) The residual form "keeps the update consistent" (l. 642-643). (c) "Together with the consistency of the residual form, zero stability is the classical basis of a convergence argument" (l. 712-714). Statement (c) does not hold under this definition: persistence is consistent in this sense and zero-stable (κ = 1), yet it does not converge. The classical argument needs the one-step error to vanish faster than Δt, so the rate must approach F. Statements (a) and (b) also read as "consistency is automatic", which §4.2.1 contradicts ("this is not automatic"; it needs a bounded or Lipschitz f_θ). That is the point the supervisor raised in SV-4.3.
- **Fix:** Give the standard definition and drop the automatic reading. At l. 533-536: "The first is \emph{consistency}: the error of one step must vanish faster than the step itself, $\lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \lVert \mathcal{A}(\Delta t, u(t)) - u(t+\Delta t) \rVert / \Delta t = 0$; for an update in residual form this requires the rate to approach the right-hand side $F$." Keep \citep{Brandstetter2022}, or cite the ODE textbook already used for the Euler step. At l. 538-539: "it returns the current state at $\Delta t = 0$ for any bounded rate." At l. 642-643: "…in the residual form of~\eqref{eq:bg:euler}, so the update reduces to the current state as the step shrinks." At l. 712: "Together with consistency (\S\ref{sec:background:pde-solvers:time}), zero stability…".
- **Also at:** 02-background.tex:539; 02-background.tex:642; 02-background.tex:712
- **Recurs:** SV-4.3

- **Status:** open

### R-0370 · S2 · §2.2.2 Stepping in time — 02-background.tex:535

~~~text
$\lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \lVert \mathcal{A}(\Delta t, u^{0}) - u(\Delta t) \rVert = 0$
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement (technical error); Guide §1 (no claims stronger than the evidence)
- **Problem:** As defined, the limit holds for every update that is continuous in Δt and returns u^0 at Δt = 0, because both A(Δt, u^0) and u(Δt) tend to u^0. The next sentence says the residual form returns the current state 'whatever the rate'. §2.3 then concludes that the residual form 'keeps the update consistent' (l. 642), and uses this consistency with zero stability as 'the classical basis of a convergence argument' (l. 712-714). Read together, any rate f, even a wrong one, would be consistent, and the convergence argument would hold for any learned operator. In numerical analysis, consistency means the one-step (local truncation) error vanishes faster than the step, ||A(Δt,u^0) - u(Δt)||/Δt -> 0. That holds only if the rate approximates F, and it is the form the Lax/Dahlquist convergence argument needs. A reviewer with a numerical background will flag this.
- **Fix:** Rewrite l. 533-539: "The first is \emph{consistency}: as the step shrinks to zero, the error of one step must vanish faster than the step itself, $\lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \lVert \mathcal{A}(\Delta t, u^{0}) - u(\Delta t) \rVert / \Delta t = 0$ \citep{Brandstetter2022}. An update written as the current state plus $\Delta t$ times a rate, as in~\eqref{eq:bg:euler}, is said to be in \emph{residual} form; it returns the current state at $\Delta t = 0$ whatever the rate, and it is consistent if, in addition, the rate approximates $F$." Add a textbook citation for the divided form (e.g. LeVeque 2007, after checking). L. 642: "The output is applied in the residual form of~\eqref{eq:bg:euler}, so the update reduces to the current state as $\Delta t \to 0$." L. 712-714: "Together with consistency, zero stability is the classical basis of a convergence argument."
- **Also at:** 02-background.tex:538; 02-background.tex:642; 02-background.tex:713
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

- **Problem:** The Background says without any condition that the residual form "keeps the update consistent" (l. 642-643, l. 712). The definition in l. 535 only asks that ‖A(Δt,u⁰) − u(Δt)‖ → 0. In l. 642-643, write "which keeps the update consistent in this sense as long as the learned rate stays bounded for small $\Delta t$ (\S\ref{sec:method:dt-residual})". In l. 712, write "Together with consistency in this sense".

### R-0403 · S2 · §2.3 Neural PDE Solvers and Surrogate Architectures — 02-background.tex:659

~~~text
$M(t, u_0) = u(t)$, and so predict the solution at any time directly
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement (inaccurate positioning against the operator literature); CLAUDE.md: DO NOT invent / cite claims
- **Problem:** The paragraph defines neural operators as maps from the initial condition to the solution at time t, in contrast to autoregressive solvers, and the next paragraph introduces the FNO and DeepONet under this heading. However, the FNO paper uses its 2-D FNO recurrently in time (previous steps to the next step) and only its 3-D variant as a direct map. This thesis also uses the FNO as a one-step update operator inside the autoregressive framework (§4.3.4). The dichotomy is taken from Brandstetter et al. (2022) but given here without a citation, and it mixes how an operator is parameterised with how it is used in time. A reader who meets the FNO arm in Chapter 4 cannot reconcile it with 'neural operators ... predict the solution at any time directly from the initial condition', nor with the temporal-extrapolation limitation attributed to it in l. 674-677.
- **Fix:** Rewrite l. 655-662: "Learned solvers also differ in how they use time. Following \citet{Brandstetter2022}, a direct approach learns a map $M: [0, T] \times \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{F}$ with $M(t, u_0) = u(t)$ and predicts the solution at any time from the initial condition. By contrast, autoregressive solvers learn the update operator $\mathcal{A}$ of~\eqref{eq:bg:update-operator} and apply it repeatedly to unroll a trajectory. The two framings concern the use of a network, not its architecture: a neural operator such as the FNO can serve as a direct map or, applied recurrently, as an update operator \citep{Li2021}, which is how it is used in this thesis (\S\ref{sec:method:family:dense})." Restrict the limitation in l. 674-677 to the direct framing.

~~~

A map conditioned on the time elapsed since each eye's own baseline is well defined. §2.4 describes three published GA models of this kind: Mai et al. Each visit-to-visit transition constitutes one step, so every intermediate visit of an eye supervises the model, and a forecast can be started from any visit. Since there is no shared temporal origin ($t = 0$) across patients, a direct map has to be conditioned on the time elapsed since each eye's own baseline, as in \citet{Mai2024} and \citet{Lachinov2024}; an autoregressive operator is conditioned on the interval between two visits instead."

### R-0422 · S2 · §2.3 Neural PDE Solvers and Surrogate Architectures — 02-background.tex:681

~~~text
shared temporal origin ($t = 0$) across patients, a direct
time-dependent mapping is ill-posed.
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Clinical reader
- **Rule:** Guide §1 (no absolute claims); judgement: contradicts the related work reported in §2.4.2 and §5.7
- **Problem:** Calling a direct time-dependent mapping 'ill-posed' is not correct for clinical data. Disease onset is not observed, but each eye has a baseline visit, and a map M(t, u_0) from that baseline state and the elapsed time is well defined. The thesis itself reports such models working on GA: Lachinov et al. (2024) evolve a baseline scan 'to any requested time point' (§2.4.2), Mai et al. (2024) predict growth from a single baseline OCT on the same cohort (§2.4.2, §5.7), and Gigon et al. (2021) give a time-to-conversion map. A clinical reader, and above all the supervisor (co-author of the first two), will read the sentence as contradicting work the thesis cites. Calling the autoregressive framing 'the natural fit' (l. 679) makes the same overstatement. The sentence also says 'across patients', but the missing origin is per eye: onset and baseline differ between the two eyes of one patient, and §2.5.1 (l. 901) says 'across eyes'.
- **Fix:** Rewrite lines 679-682: "The autoregressive framing suits clinical longitudinal data. Each visit-to-visit transition constitutes one step. The time of disease onset is not observed, so there is no shared temporal origin ($t = 0$) across eyes; a direct mapping has to take each eye's baseline visit as its origin, as the models of \S\ref{sec:background:related-work:spatial} do, whereas an autoregressive update can start from every observed visit."
- **Also at:** 02-background.tex:679
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0423 · S2 · §2.3 Neural PDE Solvers and Surrogate Architectures — 02-background.tex:683

~~~text
is set by the clinic rather than by the model, so the model has to
support as many steps as a patient's visit schedule requires.
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Clinical reader
- **Rule:** Feedback log X3 / Guide §11.5 ('X rather than Y' contrast); judgement (clinical framing)
- **Problem:** The sentence mixes two different things. The horizon of a forecast is set by the clinical question (for example one year, as in trials). The visit schedule is a property of the follow-up data. When a forecast is made for a patient, the future visits have not happened yet, and a Δt-conditioned update does not need them to reach a horizon. As written, the sentence suggests that a forecast requires the patient's future visit schedule, and the 'rather than by the model' contrast hides the actual point: a learned operator's training horizon limits a direct mapping (previous paragraph).
- **Fix:** "In addition, the clinical question sets the horizon of a forecast, and this horizon can exceed the one seen in training; an autoregressive model reaches it by applying further steps, for example one per scheduled visit."
- **Recurs:** X3 (supervisor repeat: raised one level)
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

- **Problem:** §2.2 is about PDEs and never says that, after spatial discretisation, the grid values obey a system of ordinary differential equations du/dt = f(t, u). - **Fix:** At l. 507-509: "The two parts are independent: after the spatial discretisation, the grid values obey a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs), $\mathrm{d}u/\mathrm{d}t = f(t, u)$, and any time-stepping scheme for ODEs can advance it; the choice of scheme does not change how $f$ is computed."

### R-0508 · S2 · §2.4.3 Forecasting from Irregularly Sampled Longitudinal Data — 02-background.tex:856

~~~text
on it; the operators of this thesis take the interval as an input to a
single residual step (\S\ref{sec:background:approach}).
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Examiner
- **Rule:** judgement: contradiction between places in the printed thesis (§2.4.3 vs §4.3.7 and §2.4.2)
- **Problem:** The sentence is false for part of the survey. §4.3.7 integrates the Runge–Kutta-wrapped operators, among them the finite-element networks that 'need an integrator' and the highest-scoring operator of Table 5.1. It sets their Δt entry to zero ('the operator receives no information about the length of the interval') and can split the interval into several RK4 sub-steps. So these operators neither take the interval as an input nor take a single residual step. The sentence also contradicts l. 819-821 of the same section, which relates the Runge–Kutta-integrated operators to the continuous-time formulation. And 'condition on it' versus 'take the interval as an input' is no contrast, because taking Δt as an input is conditioning on it. The problem statement repeats the narrow form: Eq. 2.8 is given as the form of every forecast, with no word on the integrated operators.

Most operators receive $\Delta t$ as an input and are applied in one residual step (Equation~\eqref{eq:bg:problem-update}), whereas the Runge--Kutta-integrated operators, among them the finite-element networks, are autonomous fields integrated over the interval (\S\ref{sec:method:family:rk}). Unlike these models, the framework is fixed and the operator inside it is exchanged." After Eq. 2.8 add: "For an operator integrated with a Runge--Kutta scheme (\S\ref{sec:method:family:rk}), $\Delta t_k f_\theta$ stands for the combined increment of the scheme over the interval."

To the author's knowledge, a learned spatial update that acts directly on the observed lesion mask and layer maps, advances them from visit to visit, and is compared across operator classes within one fixed framework has not been studied for GA."

### R-0546 · S2 · §2.5.1 Choice of the Modelling Approach — 02-background.tex:941

~~~text
exterior is healthy; both are quasi-static, and all dynamics are concentrated at the active boundary
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Clinical reader
- **Rule:** judgement: factual error and contradiction with other places in the thesis; Guide §1 (no absolute claims)
- **Problem:** For a GA clinician the tissue around a GA lesion is not healthy. The thesis says so itself: RPE–BM thickening in a rim just outside the margin (§2.1.3 (iii)), and the rim around the lesion carrying most of the predictive signal (Cluceru, §2.4.1). New, separate foci of atrophy also appear away from the lesion. §5.4 measures new atrophy more than 0.24 mm from the baseline lesion (fold medians 5–22 %), and Appendix B notes 'new separate lesions away from the existing ones'. 'All dynamics are concentrated at the active boundary' is therefore an absolute claim that the thesis's own data contradict. The bullet 'Change driven by the neighbourhood' and the step to an operator that is 'therefore local' repeat the overstatement.

Most of the change occurs at the lesion border, where the adjacent tissue is often already altered, for example by RPE–BM thickening (\S\ref{sec:background:ga-oct:disease}), and separate new foci of atrophy can also appear away from the existing lesion. To a first approximation, such behaviour is characteristic of a system governed by a temporal PDE with strong spatial localisation." In the bullet: "GA grows mainly at the margin of the lesion, while its atrophic interior changes little (Figure~\ref{fig:bg:ga-faf}). Whether a pixel becomes atrophic is assumed to depend mainly on what surrounds it, ...". At l. 952: "is therefore mainly local".

### R-0553 · S2 · §2.5.1 Choice of the Modelling Approach — 02-background.tex:952

~~~text
forward operator that maps the present state to the future state is therefore \emph{local}, but its reach must match the distance the front
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement: two claims in one subsection contradict each other; Guide §1 (no absolute claims)
- **Problem:** This paragraph concludes that the forward operator "is therefore local" and that its reach "must" match the front's movement per visit. Fifty lines later (l. 1003-1005) the same subsection says that whether a local stencil, a global operator or both is needed "is therefore not assumed here". The reader cannot tell which is the thesis's starting position, and the reach requirement is presented as fact before Chapter 5 tests it. The directions cited (towards the fovea vs the periphery, Singh et al.) are radial directions around the fovea. They are not the grid axes along which the stencils of §4.3.3 differ, so "the size and shape of their stencils" does not follow from this evidence. The pixel-spacing argument at l. 999-1003 is what motivates the stencil shape.
- **Fix:** "The forward operator that maps the present state to the future state is therefore expected to act mainly locally, and its reach would have to cover the distance the front moves between two visits, which differs between directions." Drop or reword the last sentence ("Classical solvers build such properties in explicitly through the size and shape of their stencils") so that it does not tie the stencil shape to the fovea-periphery anisotropy.
- **Also at:** 02-background.tex:1003
- **Recurs:** AI-S16
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)

- **Problem:** As a general statement this is wrong. What holds is narrower: the U-Net and the message-passing networks used here are trained at one fixed resolution and are not discretisation-independent maps between function spaces.

- **Problem:** The section says the reference mask is a manual FAF outline registered onto the OCT grid, but it never states the consequences. A clinical reader notices three. It also inherits the lower reliability of blue-light FAF near the fovea (\S\ref{sec:background:ga-oct:oct}), which matters most for subfoveal lesions such as the one in Figure~\ref{fig:data:example-state}." ### R-0657 · S2 · §3.2 State Representation — 03-data.tex:201

~~~text
along that A-scan. Together, the ten channels describe the vertical
layer structure of the retina at every en-face position. Across the
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Clinical reader
- **Rule:** Guide §1 (no absolute claims); Guide §5.8 (methods complete enough to understand and repeat)
- **Problem:** Inside a GA lesion, the photoreceptors and the RPE are lost (§2.1.3, Fig. 2.4b). The IS/OS junction, the outer-photoreceptor boundary and the two RPE boundaries therefore have no anatomical counterpart there. Inside a GA lesion, where the photoreceptors and the RPE are lost (\S\ref{sec:background:ga-oct:disease}), the outer surfaces have no anatomical counterpart, and the channels hold [needs: what the segmentation returns there]. Positions without a depth value are stored as [needs: encoding]." After the depth-range sentence, add that values outside 0-496 are surfaces placed outside the imaged volume. Add one sentence on whether the segmentation was reviewed in the atrophic areas (needs: this fact).

### R-0693 · S2 · §3.3 Spatial Standardisation and its Measured Cost — 03-data.tex:267

~~~text
Zero-padding raises a less obvious problem. Physically, a zero means
``no signal'': a mask value of 0 means not atrophic, and a layer depth
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Supervisor
- **Rule:** Guide §11.5 (no dramatic openers; fact, number, source); Guide §11.4
- **Problem:** The paragraph opens with a dramatic signpost. Its first claim ("a zero means no signal") is contradicted by its own examples, since a mask value of 0 (non-atrophic) and a depth of 0 (top of the volume) are both valid data values, not the absence of a signal. It also never states the problem it announces: padded positions look like real tissue, and after normalisation they become extreme layer values that the model is trained to reproduce. The reader has to assemble the point from five loosely linked sentences joined by "however".
- **Fix:** Rewrite the paragraph: "Zero-padding fills the missing positions with values that also occur in real data: a mask value of 0 marks non-atrophic tissue, and a layer depth of 0 lies at the top of the volume, inside the observed range of $-14$ to $499$ axial pixels. A padded position therefore cannot be told apart from a real one by its raw value. Because cropping and padding run before the normalisation statistics are computed (\S\ref{sec:data:normalization}), the padded zeros also enter the per-channel mean and standard deviation. After normalisation, the zero fill of the layer channels lies between $-2.35$ and $-2.94$ standard deviations. The loss weights these positions like any other, so the models are also trained to reproduce this fill value."
- **Recurs:** E2 (supervisor repeat: raised one level)
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0699 · S2 · §3.3 Spatial Standardisation and its Measured Cost — 03-data.tex:302

~~~text
the one-year anchor (\S\ref{sec:data:temporal}) under-measure
progression for roughly one visit in five. The censoring also limits
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement (number disagrees with §5.1.2); Guide §1 (no vague quantities)
- **Problem:** 'Roughly one visit in five' follows from no number in the paragraph: 27.3 % of visits lose lesion area and 31.1 % touch the edge. It also disagrees with §5.1.2, which counts 21 of the 75 eyes (28 %) whose lesion touches the edge at the one-year anchor, and that eye count is what the anchor metrics depend on. The sentence counts visits where the metric is per eye. In addition, the change-region Dice does not measure progression. Censoring removes the change outside the window from both the prediction and the truth, so the metric scores a truncated change region. What is biased low are areas and growth rates measured on the window.
- **Fix:** "The models are therefore trained on censored targets. At the one-year anchor, the lesion of 21 of the 75 eyes touches this edge (\S\ref{sec:experiments:protocol:metrics}). For these eyes, the change-region metrics score only the part of the change inside the window, and lesion areas and growth rates measured on the window are biased low."

### R-0785 · S2 · §4.1 Overview — 04-method.tex:31

~~~text
handled by a single-step residual update conditioned on the interval
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Supervisor
- **Rule:** Guide §5.8 (methods consistent with each other); judgement: contradicts §4.3.6-§4.3.7
- **Problem:** §4.1 lists the time handling under 'held fixed': a single-step residual update in which Δt is an input. The caption says the output 'is multiplied by Δt and added'. §4.2.1 says 'Δt therefore enters twice', and l. 37 says every operator 'returns the full predicted next state'. §4.3.6 and §4.3.7 contradict all of this for some arms. The FEN outputs a time derivative and is always integrated with RK4 in 45-day sub-steps. The RK4 arms set the Δt input to zero. So the T-FEN (the highest mean in Table 5.1) and the RK4 arms use neither the single step nor the Δt input. The chapter's argument that the time handling cannot confound the comparison therefore does not hold as written. Equation 2.8 of the problem statement has the same gap.
- **Fix:** Rewrite l. 30-31 as: "Time is handled by the residual update of~\S\ref{sec:method:dt-residual}, which scales the output of the operator by the interval between visits. By default it is applied in one step; the Runge--Kutta wrapper (\S\ref{sec:method:family:rk}), which the finite-element network always uses, integrates the same residual in sub-steps and gives the operator no $\Delta t$ input." Add the same exception to the caption: "For the finite-element network and the Runge--Kutta arms, the multiplication by $\Delta t$ is replaced by a Runge--Kutta integration over the interval (\S\ref{sec:method:family:rk})." In §4.2.1, open l. 152 with "In the default single step, $\Delta t$ enters twice". In l. 37, write "returns the full predicted next state or, for the finite-element network, its time derivative".
- **Also at:** 04-method.tex:37; 04-method.tex:93; 04-method.tex:152
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0862 · S3 · §4.2.3 Conditioning: Patient Covariates — 04-method.tex:243

~~~text
no spatial information, they act on the prediction of an operator only as
a whole and cannot point to a location on the grid or shape the lesion
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement (technically inaccurate statement about the operators)
- **Problem:** Every operator concatenates the covariates with the local state at each node or pixel and passes them through nonlinear layers. Their effect on the output therefore varies with the local state; for example, they can change how far a given boundary advances, which shapes the boundary locally. What a global scalar cannot do is carry information about where growth occurs. "act ... only as a whole" and "cannot ... shape the lesion boundary locally" misstate this, and the same argument is reused in §6.3.
- **Fix:** "Because the covariates are the same at every grid position, they carry no information about where on the grid the lesion grows; they can only modulate how an operator responds to the local state, for example how far a given boundary advances."
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0863 · S3 · §4.2.3 Conditioning: Patient Covariates — 04-method.tex:243

~~~text
no spatial information, they act on the prediction of an operator only as
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Colleague
- **Rule:** Guide §1.2.7 (no absolute claims); judgement
- **Problem:** In a nonlinear network, a global input (a constant input plane or a conditioning vector at every node) interacts with the local features. It can therefore change the output differently at different positions, including along the lesion boundary. 'Act only as a whole' and 'cannot ... shape the lesion boundary locally' contradict what an ML reader knows about conditioning inputs, and the intended point (the covariates alone cannot single out a location) gets lost.
- **Fix:** 'Because the covariates carry no spatial information, they cannot by themselves single out a location on the grid. Any local effect has to come from their interaction with the spatial state.'
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0871 · S2 · §4.2.4 Objective — 04-method.tex:297

~~~text
\mathcal{L} \;=\; \frac{1}{\bar{w}} \sum_{c=0}^{10} w_c\,
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement (factual error in an equation); Guide §5.8 (enough detail to repeat the work)
- **Problem:** With L_MSE^(c) defined as the MSE of channel c and w̄ as the mean weight, the first term is (1/w̄)·Σ_c w_c L_c. It also changes what λ_Dice = 5 means: a re-implementation from the printed equation would weight the MSE term eleven times more against the soft-Dice term. The training code divides the weighted MSE by C·w̄, which equals Σ_c w_c.
- **Fix:** Replace \frac{1}{\bar{w}} by \frac{1}{\sum_{c} w_c} and write "... w_c its weight; the sum of the weights is the denominator". Change the sentence to: "Dividing by the sum of the weights keeps the term on the scale of an unweighted MSE; with equal weights it equals the MSE averaged over the eleven channels."

### R-0896 · S3 · §4.3 The Operators — 04-method.tex:481

~~~text
This section describes the operators placed in the slot
of~\S\ref{sec:method:framework}. Each was chosen to isolate one property:
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Supervisor
- **Rule:** Guide §2.4 (one idea per sentence, no long nested sentences)
- **Problem:** Three sentences in the unit are too long to read in one pass: - The second sentence of the section opener runs to about 70 words, with a colon, six properties and seven bracketed operator lists and section references, plus the noun stack "the reach of the spatial context of one step". - The dilated-convolution sentence (780-783) stacks two consequences and a semicolon. - The autonomous-field sentence (1147-1151) ends in the unclear clause "the state still changes by the integrated rate".
- **Fix:** Opener: "Each operator was chosen to isolate one property. The graph network on two different graphs varies the reach of one step (\S\ref{sec:method:mppde}--\S\ref{sec:method:graph}), and two truncated versions of it vary the amount of spatial context (\S\ref{sec:method:family:floors}). - **Rule:** Guide §5.8 (methods detailed enough to repeat; every quantity used is described); Guide §1 (no absolute claims: a cohort statistic stated as a general fact)
- **Problem:** This is the first and only place where the per-visit lesion-front advance is quantified, and the stencil design rests on it ('The design thus derives the reach from the physical scale of the lesion'). It is never said how the advance was measured. A clinical reader cannot tell: along which axis it was measured (the caption says 'along a row', the text does not); whether it uses only visit pairs about 180 days apart or advances scaled to 180 days (l. 793 calls it 'the per-visit front advance', a different reference); which eyes and visits enter it; and whether local shrinkage of the reference masks is included. 'The GA front advances' also reads as a fact about GA in general rather than about this cohort. Later chapters quote a range of '10 to 25 columns (57 to 142 µm)' with a pointer to this section (05-experiments.tex:900-903, 06-discussion.tex:95-96), but no range is given here or anywhere else. There is also no link to the cohort growth rate of §3.1 (0.234 mm per year in square-root area), which would let a clinician check that the number is plausible.
- **Fix:** State the measurement and its scope in place, e.g. 'In this cohort, the outer edge of the GA lesion moves along a row by a median of about 12 columns (68 µm) between consecutive visits, per 180 days [needs: the exact definition: per row, outward shift of the lesion edge between consecutive visits, either restricted to pairs about 180 days apart or scaled to 180 days; which eyes and visit pairs; how shrinkage is treated]; the upper quartile is 17 columns (97 µm) and the 90th percentile 23 columns (131 µm).' Add the range quoted in §5.3.5 and §6.1 with its meaning [needs: which quantiles 10 and 25 columns are], or remove it there. Optionally add one sentence relating the advance to the square-root-area growth rate of §3.1 [needs: the conversion].
- **Also at:** 04-method.tex:793; 04-method.tex:826
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0947 · S2 · §4.3.3 Graph Construction on an Anisotropic Grid — 04-method.tex:778

~~~text
nodes at row offsets $\{-1, 0, +1\}$ and column offsets
$\{0, \pm 7, \pm 14, \pm 21\}$, excluding the node itself: 20 neighbours in
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Colleague
- **Rule:** judgement (missing caveat); Guide §5.3 (anticipate the obvious objection)
- **Problem:** Every column offset of the stencil is a multiple of seven. At any network depth, a node therefore receives information only from columns whose index differs from its own by a multiple of seven, so the lattice splits into seven interleaved sub-lattices that share weights but never exchange messages. A page earlier the section rejects the physical k-NN graph because 'the grid decomposes into 49 independent one-dimensional rows'. A reader applies the same test here, finds the same kind of decomposition, and gets no answer. The FEN paragraph does state the analogous fact for its transport mesh ('seven interleaved triangulations'), but in the FEN the free-form term on the full mesh couples the seven triangulations, and nothing plays that role for the stencil.
- **Fix:** After 'excluding the node itself: 20 neighbours in total', add: 'Because every column offset is a multiple of seven, a node exchanges messages, at any depth, only with columns whose index differs from its own by a multiple of seven. The lattice therefore splits into seven interleaved sub-lattices, 40 µm apart along a row, which share the network weights and never exchange messages.' Follow this with the reason the split is acceptable (needs: the author's reason or evidence, e.g. that neighbouring columns 5.7 µm apart carry nearly the same state, or that the rollouts show no column-periodic pattern).
- **Also at:** 04-method.tex:795; 04-method.tex:1020

### R-0950 · S3 · §4.3.3 Graph Construction on an Anisotropic Grid — 04-method.tex:790

~~~text
One hop reaches $\pm 121$\,\textmu{}m across rows and
$\pm 119$\,\textmu{}m along a row, nearly equal on both axes at about
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Clinical reader
- **Rule:** Guide §5.3 (anticipate the obvious objection); judgement (a topic set up in §2.5.1 is dropped where the design is made)
- **Problem:** §2.5.1 tells the reader that GA grows faster towards the periphery than towards the fovea, and that the reach of the operator must match a distance that 'differs between directions'. Here the stencil is made symmetric in physical distance and called 'nearly equal on both axes', as if it matched a measured advance on both axes. Three things are left unsaid. First, the advance was apparently measured along rows only (caption, l. 826). Second, across rows the reach of one row (121 µm) is simply the smallest non-zero reach the grid allows, and it already exceeds the median per-visit advance of 68 µm; vertical growth therefore shows up in the mask only as whole-row steps. Third, the direction dependence of GA growth is radial with respect to the fovea, so an axis-aligned stencil cannot represent it and leaves it to the learned messages. The caption's 'vertical' and 'horizontal' (l. 813-815) assume horizontal B-scans, an orientation the thesis never states, so 'along a row' cannot be related to anatomical directions.
- **Fix:** After '... about 120 µm per hop.' add: 'The reach is set by the advance along rows. Across rows, one row (121 µm) is the smallest non-zero reach of the grid and already exceeds the median per-visit advance. The stencil is symmetric in physical distance and does not encode the direction dependence of GA growth described in §2.5.1, which is radial with respect to the fovea; any such dependence is left to the learned message function.' In the caption, write 'Rows are horizontal B-scans' [needs: confirmation of the raster orientation], or give the orientation once in §3.1.
- **Also at:** 04-method.tex:813
- **Recurs:** AI-S16
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0962 · S2 · §4.3.4 Dense Operators: U-Net, FNO and a Local-Kernel Hybrid — 04-method.tex:866

~~~text
5:1 without removing it. The schedule was deliberately not tuned further:
a comparison model whose geometry had been optimised on this dataset would
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** Guide §5.3 (anticipate the obvious objection); judgement (fair comparison, no test split)
- **Problem:** (i) The reasoning is hard to follow. Tuning a comparison model normally makes it a stronger control, so 'would make a weaker control' needs its reason, presumably selection bias on validation folds without a test split. (ii) That reasoning applies to the canonical model too, and the asymmetry is never stated. The dilated stencil was adopted because it scored higher on the validation folds ('This result is the reason the dilated stencil is the canonical configuration', 05-experiments.tex:670). Its ±21-column reach is the best of a five-geometry ladder on the same folds. Meanwhile the U-Net pooling schedule and the FNO mode count (l. 908) were left untuned. Every result is a validation result, so the canonical score may carry a selection bias that the dense arms do not. Neither this subsection nor §6.3 says so, and a conference reviewer would raise this first.
- **Fix:** Replace the sentence by: 'The schedule was fixed before training and not tuned further, because a setting chosen on the validation folds would carry a selection bias, as there is no test split (\S\ref{sec:data:splits}).' ### R-0978 · S3 · §4.3.6 The Finite Element Network — 04-method.tex:981

~~~text
The original uses a Galerkin method with the P1 basis of piecewise-linear
hat functions, by default on a Delaunay triangulation of the observation
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Colleague
- **Rule:** Guide §11.2; Guide §2.4 (one idea per sentence)
- **Problem:** Two sentences stack six FEM terms: Galerkin method, P1 basis, hat functions, Delaunay triangulation, mass matrix and lumping. They are followed by 'The inner products are factored so that a network predicts one coefficient per cell, vertex and feature', which gives no picture of what the free-form network computes. §2.2.1 introduced the weak form and piecewise-linear basis functions, but the text never says that 'Galerkin' refers to that weak form. Yet 'the Galerkin form' becomes the name of one of the two trained transport operators (§4.3.6, Figure 4.3, §5.7.2). Later, 'lumped assembly', 'gradient coefficients are assembled in grid units' and 'differs from such a network only at the boundary' add further unexplained FEM vocabulary.
- **Fix:** Rewrite as: 'The original discretises the unknown PDE with a Galerkin method, that is, the weak form of §2.2.1 with the piecewise-linear (P1) basis functions, on a Delaunay triangulation (a standard triangulation of scattered points) of the observation points. The weak form couples the time derivatives of neighbouring nodes through the mass matrix M of inner products between basis functions. M is lumped, that is, replaced by the diagonal matrix of its row sums, so that it is trivial to invert. The inner products of the unknown dynamics with the basis functions are split into one coefficient per triangle, vertex and channel, and a network, the free-form term, predicts each coefficient from ...' Gloss 'assembly' at l. 1003 in the same way, as the summation of the triangle contributions at each node.
- **Also at:** 04-method.tex:986; 04-method.tex:1003; 04-method.tex:1006; 04-method.tex:1018
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-0991 · S3 · §4.3.6 The Finite Element Network — 04-method.tex:1041

lattice, the assembled transport operator has a purely imaginary spectrum:

~~~

~~~

### R-1026 · S4 · §4.3.7 Fixed-Step Runge–Kutta Integration — 04-method.tex:1163

~~~text
splitting the interval into more or finer steps must not change the
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement (definition inconsistent with §5.7.1); Guide §1
- **Problem:** A numerical integrator changes its prediction with the step, by an error of order h^p. What a continuous-time model requires is that predictions converge as the step shrinks, which is the definition §5.7.1 applies (C1 convergence, C2 agreement within the noise). 'Must not change' is stricter than both that test and the Ott et al. procedure described two sentences later.

### R-1080 · S3 · §5.1.2 Metrics — 05-experiments.tex:101

~~~text
shrinkage counts as predicted change and is scored against the truth, which
is consistent with the absence of a monotonic-growth constraint
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Clinical reader
- **Rule:** judgement (clinical correctness: atrophic tissue does not regenerate); Guide §5.3 (anticipate the obvious objection)
- **Problem:** The definition presents the true change region as "the change that occurred" (l. 95), and the symmetry of the score as merely "consistent" with the design. A clinical reader knows that atrophy does not regress, and §4.2.1 itself calls shrinkage "not clinically plausible". §6.3 reports that 96 % of visit pairs lose atrophic pixels along the border and calls this more consistent with annotation and registration noise. So the change region of the headline metric contains apparent regression in almost every eye, and the metric rewards a model that reproduces it. Nothing here says so, and the reader meets the caveat only in the Limitations.
- **Fix:** l. 94–96: "Applied to the change regions, the Dice score measures how well the predicted change overlaps the change between the two reference annotations; the large part of the lesion that stays the same does not enter it." l. 100–103: "Second, the metric is symmetric. A predicted shrinkage counts as predicted change and is scored against the reference, which also shrinks locally between most pairs of visits. Because atrophy does not regenerate, this apparent shrinkage is more consistent with annotation and registration noise than with regression (\S\ref{sec:discussion:limitations}). It is nevertheless part of the change region on which every operator is scored, and no monotonic-growth constraint is imposed (\S\ref{sec:method:dt-residual})."
- **Also at:** 05-experiments.tex:95
- **Recurs:** AI-S13
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

The section's thesis statement, its repetition at l. 450 ("a finite-element network, a graph network and a U-Net") and the summary at l. 503 hold only if the Runge-Kutta variant is silently left out, although l. 510 calls the RK4 runs arms. A reviewer who checks the headline against the table finds it false as written.

At l. 450: "The highest arm of each of the three leading classes is a finite-element network, a graph network and a U-Net." Make the same change at l. 503.

~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement (claim not supported by the method description in §4.3.6)
- **Problem:** §4.3.6 states that one evaluation of the FEN couples only nodes that share a triangle, that reach "has to come from sub-steps", and that the FEN always runs RK4 in 45-day steps. ### R-1202 · S2 · §5.3 Forecasts Beyond One Year — 05-experiments.tex:567

~~~text
the first year, the operators fall into three groups. The three whose
single step reaches less far than the lesion front advances between two
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Examiner
- **Rule:** judgement: the grouping is not supported by the thesis's own description of the FEN; Guide §5.8
- **Problem:** For the $k$-NN network and the one-hop floor, one step is one visit interval. For the free-form FEN, one step is a 45-day RK4 sub-step. §4.3.6 states that its "spatial reach has to come from sub-steps", and a median 180-day interval takes about four such steps of four stages each. The group therefore compares the FEN's reach per sub-step with the front's advance per visit. Per visit interval, by the thesis's own reach measure, the free-form FEN couples far more pixels than one step does. The reach explanation for its low first-year score is therefore not shown, and the same grouping is repeated in the Figure 5.3 caption and in §5.4.4.
- **Fix:** Either state the free-form FEN's reach per visit interval and argue why it still counts as short-reach (needs: hops per RK4 step × sub-steps per interval, from §4.3.6), or regroup by what is true: "The $k$-NN graph network and the one-hop floor, whose update reaches less far than the lesion front advances between two visits, and the free-form FEN score 0.388 to 0.397."

### R-1226 · S3 · §5.3 Forecasts Beyond One Year — 05-experiments.tex:609

the order changes with the horizon, and global context appears to matter
more for long forecasts than for the first year.
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Clinical reader
- **Rule:** Guide §5.3 (anticipate the obvious objection); Guide §5.4 (watch for speculation)
- **Problem:** The horizon bins hold different eyes. Only eyes followed for more than three years contribute to the last bin; follow-up ranges from 720 to 2160 days with a median of 1080 days (§3.1). Differences between bins therefore mix the horizon with which eyes are included. A clinical reader will ask whether the long-term values describe a particular subgroup, for example the eyes kept under follow-up longest. The text says only that the last bin "holds the fewest visits", then reads the change of the gaps and of the operator order across bins as an effect of the horizon ("close part of their gap", "global context appears to matter more for long forecasts").
- **Fix:** After "This last bin holds the fewest visits" add "and only the eyes followed for more than three years (needs: number of eyes per bin), so differences between bins reflect both the horizon and the eyes included." Replace the closing clause with "Among the other operators, the order changes between the bins; in the last bin the FNO lies above the U-Net."

- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-1275 · S2 · §5.4.2 Physical Reach at Lesion Scale — 05-experiments.tex:748

~~~text
The best tested reach, $\pm 21$ columns (about 119\,\textmu{}m), lies close
to the 90th percentile of the per-visit front advance, 23 columns
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement (inconsistent reach accounting); Guide §5.4 (speculation)
- **Problem:** The match with the front advance is stated per hop. The canonical network runs two message-passing rounds, however, so one update reaches ±42 columns (about 238 µm). That is about twice the 90th-percentile advance, and §5.5 itself uses 0.24 mm as the network's reach. Per update, the ±12 variant (±24 columns, about 136 µm) is the geometry that matches the 23-column advance, and it scores 0.019 lower. For the k-NN graph, the thesis counts reach per update (two rounds give ±4 columns, §4.3.3); for the stencil, §5.4.2 and §5.4.5 count it per hop. Line 903 also says "One hop ... so a single step of such an operator", which mixes the two. The ladder shows that ±21 columns per hop is the best tested geometry. It does not show that the best reach equals the front advance; that correspondence was a design input (§4.3.3).
- **Fix:** Count reach per update throughout and rewrite: "No tested geometry scores higher than the default hop of ±21 columns, which was set from the 90th percentile of the per-visit advance (§4.3.3). With two rounds, one update of the default network reaches ±42 columns (about 238 µm), about twice that advance. The ±12 variant, whose update reaches ±24 columns, scores lower." In line 903: "Two rounds on the index-space graph reach only ±4 columns, about 23 µm along a row (§4.3.3), so one update of such an operator covers only a small part of that advance."
- **Also at:** 05-experiments.tex:903; 05-experiments.tex:909; 05-experiments.tex:866; 05-experiments.tex:993

### R-1279 · S3 · §5.4.3 Global and Local Context Together — 05-experiments.tex:767

~~~text
a local path. The Fourier Neural Operator sees the whole grid in every
layer through its Fourier modes but has no local path
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement (contradicts §4.3.4); Guide §5.4
- **Problem:** §4.3.4 describes each FNO block as a spectral convolution plus a pointwise 1 × 1 path ("a local linear transform"). The FNO therefore has a local, pointwise path; what it lacks is a path over spatial neighbours. The spectral path also keeps only 14 modes, with a finest wavelength of about 500 µm along a row (§4.3.4; the mode count was not ablated). That is far coarser than the 68 µm median front advance. - **Fix:** "The Fourier Neural Operator sees the whole grid in every layer through 14 retained Fourier modes, whose finest wavelength is about 500 µm along a row (§4.3.4); its only local path is pointwise. This comparison pairs the plain FNO with the same FNO whose pointwise path is widened to a 3 × 3 convolution, which adds 800 parameters." In the conclusion, add "with 14 retained modes, a count that was not varied".

### R-1307 · S2 · §5.4.4 An Explicit Transport Term — 05-experiments.tex:863

~~~text
the one-hop floor (0.395) and the $k$-NN graph network (0.397). All three
operators reach less far in one step than the lesion front advances between
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement (contradicted by §4.3.6)
- **Problem:** §4.3.6 states that one FEN evaluation couples only nodes that share a triangle, so "spatial reach has to come from sub-steps". The FEN runs RK4 in 45-day steps. Over a 180-day interval that gives four RK4 steps of four evaluations each, i.e. up to 16 triangle hops, or about ±16 columns (about 91 µm) along a row. That is more than the 68 µm median advance. The claim is therefore unsupported for the free-form FEN if "one step" means one visit interval. If it means one evaluation, the transport term reaches only 7 columns (about 40 µm), also less than the median advance, and the reading of the T-FEN as a remedy fails instead. Either way, the reach argument does not separate the free-form FEN from the T-FEN as stated. It also leaves open why the free-form FEN scores like the k-NN network despite its wider per-visit receptive field.
- **Fix:** State each operator's reach on the same basis (per visit interval): "The two graph networks reach at most ±4 columns in one update (§4.3.3). The free-form FEN couples only neighbouring nodes per evaluation, and its RK4 sub-steps extend this to at most about ±16 columns over a 180-day interval (§4.3.6), yet it scores like the graph networks." Then describe the T-FEN by the reach of its transport mesh (7 columns per evaluation). Remove "reach less far in one step" for the FEN, here and in line 899.
- **Also at:** 05-experiments.tex:899
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

### R-1332 · S3 · §5.4.5 Summary of the Ablation Studies — 05-experiments.tex:904 (p. 61)

~~~text
the index-space graph reaches only $\pm 2$ columns, about 11\,\textmu{}m
along a row, so a single step of such an operator covers only a small part
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** Guide §4 (technical terms keep one meaning)
- **Problem:** "Reach" is defined in §2.2.1 as the distance one evaluation of the update moves information. The thesis then measures it sometimes per hop and sometimes per update (all message-passing rounds). §4.3.3 says two rounds of the index-space graph reach 4 columns (about 23 µm), and that one hop of the stencil (119 µm) matches the 90th percentile. §5.4.5 equates one hop (±2 columns, 11 µm) with "a single step". §5.4.2 and §6.1.2 say four rounds "double the reach". §5.5 uses 0.24 mm as "the reach of two message-passing rounds" and argues that "one step of the graph network does not reach that far". Chapter 7 says one step reaches as far as the front moves. Read per update, the canonical network reaches about ±238 µm, about twice the 90th-percentile advance, which a reader cannot reconcile with "one hop ... covers about the 90th percentile".

Example for §5.4.5: "One hop on the index-space graph reaches only ±2 columns, about 11 µm along a row, and one update with two rounds about 23 µm, so a single step of such an operator covers only a small part of that advance." In §5.5: "... because the graph network does not reach that far in one update (two rounds)." In Chapter 7: "so that one hop reaches about as far as the front moves between visits".

### R-1336 · S1 · §5.4.5 Summary of the Ablation Studies — 05-experiments.tex:915

~~~text
(\S\ref{sec:experiments:main-results}). That two unrelated constructions
aimed at the same limit reach about the same score is the central
~~~

- **Reviewers:** External reviewer
- **Rule:** judgement (claim contradicted by §4.3.6); Guide §5.4 (tone down what the data do not carry)
- **Problem:** §4.3.6 states that the transport term of the T-FEN runs on its own coarser mesh, seven interleaved triangulations that each connect every seventh column, and calls it "the finite-element counterpart of the dilated stencil". The free-form control uses only the full-resolution mesh. So the T-FEN comparison adds an advection mechanism and dilated connectivity at the same time, and both routes rely on a spacing of seven columns. The two constructions are therefore related, and part of their agreement is built into the design. The sentence calls this agreement the central architectural result of the survey, and §4.3.6 contradicts it.
- **Fix:** Name the shared spacing and scope the claim: "Two constructions remove this limit. The dilated stencil places the neighbours of the graph network at lesion scale, so that one hop spans 21 columns (§5.4.2). The transport term of the T-FEN moves the state along a learned velocity on a mesh that connects every seventh column (§4.3.6). Each is established against its own control, and the two arms lie within about 0.017 of each other as the two highest arms of Table 5.1 (§5.2). That a graph with dilated edges and a transport term on a dilated mesh reach about the same score is consistent with the reach explanation. The transport comparison does not separate the transport mechanism from the coarser mesh on which it runs." Drop "unrelated". If a T-FEN with transport on the full-resolution mesh exists, report it here (needs: that run).
- **Also at:** 05-experiments.tex:908

- **Status:** open

~~~

- **Reviewers:** Clinical reader
- **Rule:** Guide §11.2 (term defined for a clinical reader); judgement (clinical meaning of the measure)
- **Problem:** To an ophthalmologist, 'new atrophy far from the existing lesion' and 'distant atrophy' read as new, separate atrophic foci (multifocal GA). The 0.24 mm cut does not isolate them. The spacing between B-scans is 121.18 µm (§3.1), so new atrophy on the second B-scan beyond the baseline edge already counts as 'far'. One year of margin growth at the 90th-percentile 180-day advance (131 µm, §4.3.3) is about 0.26 mm. The share therefore mixes fast margin growth with new foci. The reach explanation fits the first. For the second, reach alone cannot place a lesion that arises away from the margin.
- **Fix:** Add after the definition: "The share includes both margin growth beyond 0.24\,mm (across rows, already the second B-scan beyond the baseline edge) and new atrophic foci separate from the baseline lesion; the analysis does not separate the two." Alternatively, report the split (needs: share of far new atrophy that is not connected to the baseline lesion), and call it 'new atrophy more than 0.24 mm from the baseline lesion' instead of 'distant atrophy'.

### R-1449 · S3 · §5.6.1 Time Handling — 05-experiments.tex:1124

~~~text
\citep{Brandstetter2022}. As a consequence, $f_\theta$ cannot be read as a
growth rate; whether the operator can be read as a continuous-time model
~~~

- **Reviewers:** Copy editor
- **Rule:** Guide §2.4 (simple sentences, clear links); Guide §4 (word repeated within a sentence)
- **Problem:** 'As a consequence' directly follows the sentence on why the multiplication is kept (persistence limit, MP-PDE form). It therefore reads as a consequence of keeping that form, while it actually follows from the internal division two sentences earlier. This is the antecedent ambiguity AI-5c.7 flagged: 'It' was replaced, but the sentence order was not changed. 'read as' also still appears twice in one sentence, and a semicolon joins two separate points.
- **Fix:** With the multiplication, $f_\theta$ must therefore output the distance divided by $\Delta t$, and the operator learns this division internally. For this reason, $f_\theta$ cannot be read as a growth rate. The multiplication changes how the same prediction is parameterised. It is kept because the prediction then falls back to the current state as $\Delta t$ approaches zero (under the assumption of~\S\ref{sec:method:dt-residual}), and because it is the form MP-PDE uses \citep{Brandstetter2022}. Whether the operator can be interpreted as a continuous-time model is tested in~\S\ref{sec:experiments:validity:swap}.
- **Recurs:** AI-5c.7
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

~~~

- **Reviewers:** Colleague
- **Rule:** Guide §2.4 (clarity); judgement: ambiguous wording
- **Problem:** "Raising the penalty" reads as "increasing the penalty weight", which is not meant. The intended point is that correcting the pixel lowers the mask where the previous state is atrophic, so the penalty grows. The paragraph then concludes only that the penalty "acts differently" on unrolled steps. The reader is left without the actual consequence: on unrolled steps the penalty keeps the model's own false positives.
- **Fix:** "If the model wrongly marked a pixel as atrophic, correcting it lowers the mask where the previous state is atrophic, so the penalty grows. A direct computation ... so the total gradient points away from the ground truth. On unrolled steps the penalty therefore keeps the model's own false positives instead of correcting them."
- **Also at:** 05-experiments.tex:1287
- **Note:** verification incomplete (a verifier failed)
- **Status:** open

~~~
